title: Autoscale cost-smoothing and tenant guardrails (PRD sketch)
content:
Purpose:
This document captures a product proposal for a cost-aware autoscaler for Dedicated capacity that provides smoother scale-up/scale-down behavior, explicit short-lived burst lanes, and tenant guardrails for fairness and isolation. The goal is to reduce cost volatility, avoid thrash on heavy tail traffic, and give platform operators predictable controls to enforce SLAs and burst policies.

Context and motivation:
- Current dedicated autoscaling reacts aggressively to short bursts; this creates oscillation and increases instance churn, prewarm overhead, and per-token cost.
- Customers need: predictable billing envelopes, bounded latency violations during spikes, and stronger controls for tenant isolation and emergency throttling.
- We want a single autoscaling system that supports: baseline reservation, ephemeral burst lanes, cost-aware smoothing, tenant fairness tokens, and operator overrides. This complements existing reserve/burst docs but focuses on scale dynamics and economic smoothing rather than capacity topology.

Key user stories:
1) As a platform owner, I want the autoscaler to avoid frequent scale-downs during short dips so we don't constantly pay prewarm penalties.
2) As a product engineer for a tenant, I want the system to allow controlled short bursts without impacting other tenants' baseline latency.
3) As an SRE, I want metrics and tooling to debug why capacity changed and which policy triggered it.
4) As a customer, I want predictable billing behavior so that transient bursts don't create unexpectedly high invoices.

Principles and constraints:
- Preserve latency SLOs for baseline and high-tier customers where possible.
- Make cost impact visible and controllable (cost attribution per-tenant, per-lane).
- Minimize complexity in the control plane (operators should be able to reason about policies).
- Designs must work across Hosted, Dedicated, Private (same primitives, different defaults).

Product features (proposal):
1) Cost-aware smoothing window
- Autoscaler maintains two time horizons: short_window (e.g., 30s–2m) for latency-sensitive upscales, and smoothing_window (e.g., 10–30m) for scale-down decisions.
- Scale-ups can be fast within limits; scale-downs are gated by the smoothing_window to avoid thrash.
- A cost budget model calculates expected marginal cost of a scale action (prewarm cost + expected run time). The scaler defers scale-downs when the projected cost > threshold.
- Configurable per-tenant smoothing multipliers to support bursty customers.

2) Ephemeral burst lanes (short-lived reserved slices)
- Create explicit burst lanes (a soft reservation of N GPUs or % of pool) that can be consumed for T minutes per policy.
- Burst lanes have three properties: duration_budget (minutes/day), concurrency_limit, and preemption_priority.
- Default behavior: low-priority burst lanes are preemptible and will be evicted first; high-priority burst lanes (paid) have stronger eviction protection.
- Consumption tracked via per-tenant ledger (used for billing and enforcement).

3) Tenant guardrails and fairness tokens
- Introduce fairness tokens: a lightweight credit that accrues slowly during idle capacity and is spent on bursts. Tokens can be used to throttle or permit requests when contention occurs.
- Guardrails enforce per-tenant max concurrent requests and token-based burst amplification.
- Admins can configure emergency caps, per-tenant throttles, and tenant isolation groups (no cross-eviction within a group).

4) Predictive prewarm and warmpool tuning
- Use traffic histograms (by tenant, model, sequence length) to prewarm KVCaches and model instances proactively for tenants with consistent diurnal patterns.
- Warmpool size adjustments consider cost tradeoff: keep warm nodes only when expected cost of cold starts > cost of warm nodes.

5) Cost attribution and owner-visible signals
- Break down cost per scale action: prewarm bytes, idle GPU minutes, tokenized inference cost. Add a per-tenant estimated delta to invoices for burst usage.
- Expose decision trace logs: which policy made the last scale decision, estimated cost calculation, expected impact window.

Operational behavior and heuristics:
- Scale-up: fast path within burstable headroom (cold start optimized), but with rate limits to avoid mass provisioning across tenants simultaneously.
- Scale-down: requires smoothing_window to have been satisfied plus negative trend signal for utilization. Optionally allow immediate scale-down when operator explicitly triggers an emergency reclaim.
- Contention resolution: when multiple tenants request burst lanes and capacity is constrained, apply ordering: (1) paid high-priority bursts, (2) tokens, (3) baseline QoS via queueing.

APIs and config knobs (customer and operator):
- Customer-facing: burst_profile (duration_budget, concurrency_limit, priority), smoothing_preference (aggressive | default | conservative), prewarm_hint (sample_rate), opt_out_flags.
- Operator-facing: global_smoothing_window, default_burst_quota, eviction_policy, cost_threshold.

Metrics and SLOs to monitor:
- autoscaler:scale_up_events_per_minute, scale_down_events_per_hour, scale_thrash_index (ratio of immediate scale-downs within smoothing_window).
- cost: prewarm_cost_per_tenant, burst_cost_per_tenant, estimated_vs_actual_invoice_delta.
- fairness: token_spend_rate, token_balance_distribution, number_of_evictions_by_tenant.

Rollout plan (phased):
- Phase 0 (experiment): implement smoothing_window logic and add decision trace logs in a test cluster. Instrument metrics. (INF-2467)
- Phase 1 (beta): add ephemeral burst lanes with simple duration_budget enforcement, expose customer API flags for a handful of pilot tenants. Monitor cost attribution and tenant QoS.
- Phase 2 (expanded): add fairness tokens, predictive prewarm integration, and per-tenant cost dashboards.
- Phase 3 (GA): enable defaults for new Dedicated customers; provide migration guidance for existing contracts.

Open design questions / tradeoffs:
- How to price burst lanes fairly across committed vs non-committed customers? (billing complexity vs simplicity)
- Token accrual rate: should tokens be proportional to baseline reservation or absolute?
- Warmpool sizing: how aggressive can we be without requiring large reserved capacity across all customers?
- Failure modes: how to avoid cascading prewarm storms when many tenants receive same pattern predictions?

Implementation notes (engineering hints):
- Keep control-plane state minimal: store short-lived leases for burst lanes, tokens as counters, and amortized cost estimates.
- Start with a deterministic policy that can be tuned remotely rather than a black-box ML controller.
- Integrate with existing routing/fallback layer so bursts can fall back to cheaper model variants or lower-precision paths when capacity constrained.
- Add a simulation harness (simple traffic replay) to validate smoothing window and burst policies before rollout.

UX and billing implications:
- Billing needs a clear line item for burst consumption (minutes, nodes) and for prewarm amortization.
- Console: add burst dashboard with current usage, remaining duration_budget, and token balance. Provide a way to request temporary priority increases (approval flow).

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: complexity leads to operator confusion. Mitigation: ship sane defaults and high-visibility tracing + one-click rollback.
- Risk: unfairness between tenants. Mitigation: tokenization + visibility + conservative default quotas.
- Risk: cost underestimation for prewarm-heavy workloads. Mitigation: conservative cost model and billing alerts.

Next steps / TODOs:
- Align on smoothing_window defaults and cost_threshold math (action: simulation with historical tenant traces) — Assignee: Luca Martell — JIRA:DEDI-812
- Prototype ephemeral burst lane ledger and token counters in staging — Assignee: Priya Singh
- Wire decision traces to autoscaler API and add dashboard panels — Assignee: Arjun Patel
- Prepare pilot selection criteria and customer communications (pricing and limits) — Assignee: Devon Lee

Related docs and references:
- Capacity reserve playbooks (see product/dedicated/*)
- Prior autoscaler notes: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/DED/Autoscaler+Design+Notes
- Billing/ledger model proposals: JIRA:BILL-121

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally a sketch: looking for feedback on the token model, burst duration budgets, and the tradeoff curve between prewarm cost and smoothing aggressiveness.
- If you have tenant traces that show 1–15 minute microbursts please attach them to JIRA:DEDI-812 so we can validate default windows.
